G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T
• O3 nanobubbles boost methane yield 
from swine wastewater by 87.5%
• Nanobubbles accelerate hydrolysis and 
acidification in anaerobic digestion.
• Nanobubbles enriched microbes and 
boosted methanogenic pathways.
• Charged nanobubbles may act as abiotic 
mediator for electron transfer.

Methanogenesis
A B S T R A C T
Swine wastewater contains recoverable energy, but anaerobic digestion is often limited by complex organics and 
slow hydrolysis. To overcome this limitation, this study introduced nanobubble technology using three gas media 
(air, O2, and O3) and systematically studied their effects on methane recovery during the anaerobic digestion of 
swine wastewater. Batch experiments showed that O3 nanobubbles achieved the strongest enhancement, 
increasing cumulative methane production by 87.5% compared with the control. This improvement may result 
from the strong oxidative capacity of O3 nanobubbles to degrade recalcitrant organics, as indicated by the second 
methane production peak observed only in the O3 nanobubbles. In contrast, O2 nanobubbles provided the 
weakest improvement, potentially because excess dissolved oxygen stimulated facultative aerobic respiration,

Overall, O3 nanobubbles show promise for resource recovery from organic waste.
1. Introduction
The rapid expansion and intensive development of the swine in­
dustry in recent years have led to increased pollution of swine waste­
water (SW). Although this type of wastewater contains large amounts of 
recoverable organic matter, it also harbors toxic substances and patho­
gens (Zhang et al., 2021). Improper treatment not only wastes biological 
resources but also pollutes the environment and endangers human 
health. Therefore, the selection of appropriate methods is critical to SW 
disposal in an environmental-friendly and cost-efficient way. Anaerobic 
digestion (AD) represents an efficient swine manure treatment tech­
nology capable of simultaneously removing pollutants and recovering 
resources (Massalha et al., 2020). However, the presence of substances 
that are difficult to degrade such as cellulose and lignin in SW leads to 
inefficient hydrolysis, low methane yield, and long digestion time (Li 
et al., 2020). To enhance the AD efficiency of SW, various strategies have 
been explored, such as thermal pretreatment, integration with microbial 
electrolysis systems, and co-digestion (Wang et al., 2020c). However, 
these methods often have certain limitations, including high energy 
requirements and complex operation demands (Yang et al., 2019). 
Therefore, there is increasing interest in developing alternative tech­
nologies that are efficient, environmentally friendly, and easily inte­
grated into existing AD systems.
In recent years, nanobubble (NB) technology has emerged as a 
promising approach for wastewater treatment, with its application scope 
covering livestock and agricultural wastewater. NBs are tiny bubbles 
with a diameter of less than 1 μm, possessing unique physical and 
chemical properties, such as high specific surface area, efficient gas 
solubility, excellent stability, and prolonged residence times in water 
(over 14 days) (Wang et al., 2019). NBs have the advantages of high 
efficiency, low-cost, and the absence of secondary pollution (Yang et al., 
2019), and thus are widely used in AD processes. NBs can significantly 
enhance the gas–liquid mass transfer efficiency and generate free radi­
cals (Yang et al., 2019), thereby effectively promoting the hydrolysis of 
particulate organic matter, improving microbial substrate accessibility, 
and stimulating microbial metabolism during the biological treatment. 
Moreover, NBs can significantly affect the redox process. NBs can pro­
duce reactive oxygen species, which help optimize redox potential 
during denitrification and facilitate sulfide oxidation/reduction to 
mitigate hydrogen sulfide inhibition. Studies have shown that nano­
bubble water (NBW) generated from gases such as air, nitrogen, and 
carbon dioxide can effectively enhance the AD of recalcitrant organic 
matter (Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2020a). For instance, using 
cellulose, lignin, and residual activated sludge as substrates, the 
methane yield in the N2-NBW group increased by 9%, 22%, and 29%, 
respectively, compared to the untreated group (Wang et al., 2020b; Yang 
et al., 2019). Among various gases used for NBs generation, O3 has 
attracted considerable attention due to its strong oxidation capacity and 
ability to enhance the biodegradability of complex organic substrates. 
However, conventional O3 processes often suffer from low gas utiliza­
tion efficiency and high operational costs, primarily due to rapid ozone 
decomposition and limited mass transfer. Studies have shown that the 
ozone transfer efficiency in conventional gas bubbling systems is 
generally below 20–30% (Gottschalk, 2008), necessitating relatively 
high O3 dosages. Integrating O3 with NB technology offers a potential 
strategy to overcome these limitations. NB technology generates 
nanoscale bubbles (diameter < 1 μm) with extremely large specific 
surface areas and prolonged residence times in water. These character­
istics substantially enhance ozone utilization efficiency, enabling 
effective oxidation at lower ozone concentrations while reducing gas 
loss and operational energy consumption. Furthermore, NB generation 
systems do not require complex aeration devices inside the reactor and 
can alleviate the burden on off-gas treatment systems, thereby simpli­
fying the overall reactor configuration. Previous studies have applied 
NBs ozonation as a pretreatment step for wastewater treatment. For 
example, O3 NBs have been used to oxidatively degrade high concen­
trations of oxytetracycline (Zhou et al., 2024) and to treat ibuprofen- 
containing pharmaceutical wastewater (Zhou et al., 2025), thereby 
reducing toxicity and improving the performance of subsequent AD. 
However, these studies primarily focused on O3 pretreatment prior to 
digestion, while the direct application of O3 NBs within the anaerobic 
digestion process remains largely unexplored.
Therefore, this study aims to systematically elucidate the mechanism 
of action of NBW to promote the performance of AD, with a focus on 
revealing its microbial and metabolic regulatory mechanisms. This study 
aims to investigate the effects of NBW generated from different gas 
sources (air, O2, and O3) on the methane production performance during 
AD. Secondly, we studied the dynamic changes in the microbial com­
munity, focusing on how the addition of NBs reshapes the composition 
and enriches key functional microorganisms during the hydrolysis, 
acidification, and methanogenesis. Then, this study elucidates the 
metabolic coordination promoted by NBs, particularly emphasizing its 
function as an abiotic mediator facilitating direct interspecies electron 
transfer (DIET). By combining performance data with metagenomic 
data, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of the bio­
physical and biochemical processes driving enhanced methane 
recovery.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Preparation and characterization of nanobubble water
NBW was generated using a NB generator (NANOTM MF-5000, 
China) following the manufacturer’s instructions and a previously re­
ported procedure (Wang et al., 2018). During operation, the liquid flow 
rate was maintained at 8 L/min and the gas flow rate was set at 0.5 L/h. 
The gas and deionized water were simultaneously pumped into the 
generator for 20 min. Three types of gases were applied in this study, 
including laboratory air, high-purity O2 (99.99%), and high-purity O3 
(99.99%). Accordingly, the resulting NBW samples were denoted as Air- 
NBW, O2-NBW, and O3-NBW, respectively. The particle size distribution 
and number concentration of NBs in each type of NBW were determined 
in triplicate prior to use using a nanoparticle tracking analysis system 
(NanoSight NS500, Malvern Instrument Ltd., UK). To evaluate the sta­
bility of NBW, all three NBW samples were stored at ambient tempera­
ture for 48 days, during which NB size and concentration were 
monitored daily.
2.2. Batch AD experiment
2.2.1. Raw swine wastewater and inoculum
The raw SW used in this study was collected from a large-scale pig

farm in Beijing, China, and was stored at 4℃ after collection. The SW 
had a volatile solids/ total solids (VS/TS) ratio of 43.38%, an ammonia 
nitrogen (TAN) concentration of 453.7 ± 9.3 mg-N/L, a soluble chem­
ical oxygen demand (SCOD) of 3306.7 ± 244.9 mg/L, and a pH of 8.2 
(Table S1). The anaerobic inoculum was obtained from a laboratory- 
scale anaerobic reactor that had been operating stably for an extended 
period. The inoculum exhibited high stability and low background ac­
tivity, with the following primary physicochemical properties: a VS/TS 
ratio of 41.44%, a TAN concentration of 41.3 mg-N/L, a SCOD of 832 
mg/L, and a pH of 8.48 (Table S1). The low organic content and mature 
microbial community of the inoculum ensured minimal endogenous 
methane production during the BMP assays.
2.2.2. Batch AD test
Batch anaerobic digestion assays were conducted using an AMPTS II 
system (AMPTS II, Bioprocess Control AB, Sweden) in accordance with 
the standard biochemical methane potential (BMP) testing protocol. 
Scott Duran bottles with a total working volume of 500 mL were 
employed as AD reactors. For each reactor, 242  mL of substrate and 58 
mL of inoculum were added, resulting in a VS ratio of 1:1.03 and a TS 
ratio of 1:1.06, followed by the addition of 100 mL of either deionized 
water, Air-NBW, O2-NBW, or O3-NBW. The experimental groups are 
named Air-NBW, O2-NBW, and O3-NBW, with DW (deionized water) 
used as the control group, and the detailed operating conditions are 
listed in Table S2. All treatments were performed in triplicate. To 
establish anaerobic conditions, each reactor was purged with high- 
purity nitrogen gas (99.99%) for 5 min before sealing. Subsequently, 
the reactors were incubated in a thermostatic water bath at 37 ± 1℃ for 
28 days, with continuous stirring at 120 rpm. Each bottle was equipped 
with a liquid sampling port and a gas outlet. Liquid samples (10 ml) were 
withdrawn on days 0, 7, 14, 21, and 28 and stored at −20℃ prior to 
analysis. The gas outlet of each reactor was connected to an absorption 
bottle containing 3 M NaOH solution to remove CO2. Methane produc­
tion was continuously monitored using an online gas measurement 
system. All methane yields were normalized to standard temperature 
and pressure (273.15 K and 1 atm) and expressed based on the VS 
content of the SW added to the reactors.
2.2.3. Physicochemical analysis
TS, VS, total nitrogen (TN) and TAN were determined by standard 
analytical methods (Fan et al., 2020). pH was determined by a pH meter 
(SenTix® 940–3, WTW, Germany). For the determination of SCOD, the 
samples were first filtered through 0.45 μm filter membrane, and then 
quantitatively analyzed by using Hach reagent tubes. The volatile fatty 
acid (VFA) was determined by centrifugation, filtration through 0.22 μm 
filter membrane, and the filtrate was acidified by 5% sulfuric acid, and 
then analyzed by gas chromatograph (Agilent GC-6890 N, Agilent 
Technologies, USA) with a hydrogen flame ionization detector and a DB- 
FATWAX UI column (30 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 µm, Agilent Technologies, 
USA). The temperatures of both the injector and detector were set at 
250℃, with a split ratio of 25:1. The oven temperature program was as 
follows: initially held at 80℃ for 1  min, then ramped to 200℃ at a rate 
of 10 ℃/min. The injection volume was 0.5 µL. Nitrogen was used as the 
carrier gas at a flow rate of 25 mL/min.
2.3. DNA extraction and metagenomic sequencing
The total genomic DNA of the samples was extracted by FastDNA 
SPIN kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals, USA), and the operation was strictly 
followed the instructions of the kit. The concentration and purity of the 
DNA were detected by NanoDrop spectrophotometer (NanoDrop ND- 
1000, Thermo Scientific, USA), and the integrity of the DNA was veri­
fied by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis. Metagenomic sequencing was 
performed by Majorbio, and the sequencing platform was Illumina 
HiSeq 2000. In order to construct the paired-end library construction, 
the genomic DNA was firstly broken to the average fragment length of 
about 400 bp by Covaris ultrasonicator (M220, Covaris Inc., USA). Then, 
the library was constructed by using NEXTFLEX™ Rapid DNA-Seq kit 
(Bioo Scientific, USA), and then amplified by bridge PCR, and then 
sequenced by using NovaSeq or HiSeq X reagent kits (Illumina, USA). 
The raw sequence data reported in this paper have been deposited in the 
NCBI database (PRJNA1438379).
2.4. Bioinformatic analysis
The raw sequencing reads were quality filtered by fastp software 
(https://github.com/OpenGene/fastp) to obtain high quality clean 
reads. The clean reads were spliced into overlapping clusters by 
MEGAHIT software (https://github.com/voutcn/megahit), and the 
minimum length threshold of overlapping clusters was set to 300 bp 
during the splicing process. Based on the spliced overlap clusters, Met­
aGene software (https://metagene.cb.k.u-tokyo.ac.jp/) was used to 
complete the prediction of open reading frames (ORFs). The redundant 
sequences were clustered using CD-HIT software (https://www.bioinfor 
matics.org/cd-hit/), and the sequence identity and coverage cutoffs 
were both set at 90%, and the longest sequence in each cluster was 
selected to construct a nonredundant gene catalog. The nonredundant 
gene catalog was compared with the NR database and the Kyoto Ency­
clopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database, and the functional 
annotation and species classification annotation of the genes were 
completed by BLASTP software (version 2.2.28+; E-value ≤1E −
5). 
Subsequent annotation analysis and downstream data analysis were 
completed on the Majorbio BioCloud platform (https://cloud.majorbio. 
com/). Gene abundance was calculated based on the number of read 
segments aligned to each gene, and relative abundance was expressed as 
the ratio of the number of read segments aligned to the target gene to the 
total number of read segments in a single sample. Annotation and 
downstream analyses were further performed using the Majorbio Cloud 
Platform (https://cloud.majorbio.com/). Gene abundance was calcu­
lated based on the number of reads mapped to each gene, and relative 
abundance was expressed as the proportion of reads assigned to a given 
gene relative to the total reads per sample.
2.5. Statistical analysis
Differences in microbial community composition of the samples at 
the phylum level were analyzed by performing principal component 
analysis (PCA) in the vegan package of the R software. Heatmaps of the 
distribution of functional genes involved in each metabolic pathway at 
different AD stages were done by the online tool ClustVis. The initial 
processing of the experimental raw data was done using Microsoft Excel 
2019 software. Differences in cumulative methane production between 
treatment groups were tested by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) 
and Tukey HSD, which was analyzed in IBM SPSS Statistics version 22.0, 
setting P < 0.05 as statistically significant difference. Curve fitting and 
result visualization were achieved by Origin 2019b software. Differ­
ences between groups in the relative abundance of functional genes 
were analyzed by chi-square test, and P < 0.05 was used as the criterion 
to determine that the differences were statistically significant.
3. Results
3.1. Physicochemical properties of nanobubble water
In this study, NBW was prepared by a NB generator, and the char­
acteristic indexes of the produced NBs are shown in Fig. 1. The size of 
NBs in the three types of NBW is mainly distributed between 100–300 
nm, of which the average diameters of Air NBs, O2 NBs, and O3 NBs are 
177.5 ± 15.1 nm, 170.0 ± 31.3 nm, and 171.8 ± 30.2 nm in that order; 
and the corresponding total number of bubbles of 2.5 × 107, 2.1 × 107, 
and 2.2 × 107 particles/mL, respectively, which are similar to the results 
reported in existing studies (X. Wang et al., 2020b). Statistical analysis

showed that there was no significant difference in the average particle 
size and number of the three NB preparations (P > 0.05). This physical 
consistency ensures comparability between different treatments. 
Consequently, observed differences in methane recovery primarily stem 
from the chemical composition and oxidation capacity of the gas, rather 
than the physical properties of the NBs. This result is consistent with the 
conclusion of the previous study that the particle size distribution and 
concentration of NBs tend to stabilize without significant fluctuation 
when the preparation duration of NBs exceeds 20 min (Wang et al., 
2019).
In this study, the retention capacity and stability performance of NBs 
in aqueous solutions were evaluated by a 48-day storage test, and the 
changes in bubble particle size and number were monitored (Fig. 1B). 
The particle size and concentration of Air NB and O2 NB remained 
relatively stable during the first 14 d of storage; after 14 d, the con­
centration of the NBs decreased, and the average particle size tended to 
increase. Even with the above changes, the concentrations of the two 
types of NBs remained in the order of 107 particles/mL, and the particle 
sizes were basically in the range of 186–337 nm. In contrast, the con­
centration of O3 NBs showed fluctuations during the storage period, with 
values ranging from 2.2 × 107 to 1.2 × 108 particles/mL, a phenomenon 
that may be related to the instability of O3 itself. However, the average 
particle size of O3 NBs remained relatively stable throughout the storage 
period, basically around 200 nm (Fig. 1B). The above results demon­
strate the successful generation characteristics and storage performance 
of the prepared NBW in aqueous solution, providing a useful 
physicochemical basis for its subsequent application in the AD system. 
However, under the complex digestion matrix, the behavior of NBs, 
particularly their size evolution and concentration dynamics, remains to 
be further elucidated using more targeted analytical approaches.
All three NB types showed long-term stability, consistent with re­
ports that NBs can persist in water for over 14 days (Ji et al., 2020; Liu 
et al., 2016). This stability is mainly explained by their physicochemical 
features: (i) nanoscale size gives very low buoyancy and a slow rise 
velocity (Favvas et al., 2021); and (ii) a strongly negative zeta potential 
(typically −15 to −30 mV) creates an interfacial electric double layer 
(Varoutoglou et al., 2025), whose electrostatic repulsion inhibits coa­
lescence and collapse (Wang and Lu, 2025). These properties ensured 
stable NB presence throughout the AD tests.
3.2. The influence of nanobubble water on methane production 
performance
The impact of NBW addition on methanogenic performance was 
evaluated in batch anaerobic digestion experiments. As shown in 
Fig. 2A, NBW significantly enhanced the cumulative methane yield 
compared to the DW (P < 0.05). The cumulative methane production of 
O3-NBW, Air-NBW, and O2-NBW were 143.0 ± 3.7, 109.0 ± 6.1, and 
94.1 ± 3.0 NmL/g-VS, respectively, increased by 87.5%, 43.0%, and 
23.4% compared with DW (76.2 ± 3.7 NmL/g-VS). The COD balance 
analysis also demonstrates that NBs promote methane production 
(Table S3, Text S1). In the O3-NBW, approximately 28.8% of the total 
COD was converted to methane, which is higher than DW. The con­
version of COD from the solid/liquid to the gas indicates that NBs 
facilitate the mineralization of organic matter.
The trend of daily methane production was similar for all experi­
mental groups, but the peak methane production appeared earlier and 
peaked higher in the NBW treatments, while the DW did not show this 
feature (Fig. 2B). In addition, with the addition of NBW, the peak of 
daily methane production appeared earlier and the duration of the high 
methane production state was prolonged, a phenomenon that effectively 
shortened the stagnation phase at the beginning of the reaction startup 
(Fig. 2B). Of interest, the O3-NBW showed two distinct peaks in daily 
methane production, the first peak is presumed to be associated with the 
rapid degradation and fermentation of readily biodegradable organics, 
whereas the second peak may be attributed to the subsequent oxidative 
decomposition of refractory organics induced by O3 NBs to be converted 
into substances that can be utilized by microorganisms and metabolized 
for methane production (Lu et al., 2020).
3.3. Changes in soluble organic matter and volatile fatty acids
In addition to the methanogenic process, the effect of NBW on the 
conversion of organic matter in the AD was also reflected in the changes 
in the content of SCOD and VFA (Fig. 2C-D, Table S4). During days 0–7, 
SCOD undergoes rapid depletion, indicating that SCOD are rapidly 
transformed during the early stages of AD. This signifies the presence of 
active hydrolysis and acidification processes. It is noteworthy that the 
SCOD removal efficiencies of the reactors in all NBW treatments were 
higher than DW, with the removal rates of the O3-NBW, Air-NBW, and 
O2-NBW ranging from 84.6% to 85.8%, which were clearly higher than 
those of DW (78.7%). Secondly, the addition of NBW promoted the 
turnover of VFAs. In the early stage of hydrolytic acidification of AD 
(0–7 d), the accumulation of VFA was higher in the NBW treatments. 
VFA concentration peaked on the seventh day. Although alkalinity was 
not directly measured, the pH in the reactor remained between 7.9 and 
8.1, indicating no acidification occurred during digestion. After entering 
the stage of 7–14 d, VFA began to be rapidly consumed, and this process 
was concomitant with the active period of methanogenesis, and the 
change was most significant in the O3-NBW. Critically, this rapid turn­
over process of VFAs is synchronized with methanogenesis, suggesting 
that NBW drives the methanogenic process by increasing the turnover

In addition, at the late stage of AD (14–28 d), the TAN was higher in 
NBW treatments than in the control DW (Fig. S1A). The increase in TAN 
concentration may be associated with the mineralization of nitrogen- 
containing organic compounds a common process during anaerobic 
digestion (Yang et al., 2019). It is noteworthy that no ammonia inhibi­
tion occurred in all reactors due to low TAN concentrations (less than 
1700 mg-N/L), which might be attributed to the low concentration of TS 
in this study (Fan et al., 2020). Similarly, the pH value in all groups 
gradually increased after the initial decline due to VFAs converted to 
methane (Fig. S1B), indicating that the AD process was not inhibited by 
VFAs accumulation. The concentration of free ammonia nitrogen (FAN) 
was calculated based on TAN and pH (Text S2), the FAN concentration 
ranged from 38.3 to 84.8 mg-N/L during digestion (Table S5). On Day 
0 of digestion, the highest FAN concentration (84.8 mg-N/L) was 
observed in the O2-NBW reactor, followed by 79.4 mg-N/L in the O3- 
NBW reactor on Day 28. Previous studies indicate that FAN concentra­
tions below 150–200 mg-N/L do not usually produce a significant 
inhibitory effect (Rajagopal et al., 2013; Yenigün and Demirel, 2013). 
Therefore, in this study, FAN inhibition is unlikely to significantly affect 
methane production.
3.4. Characterization of microbial communities
In order to clarify the correlation between methanogenesis and mi­
crobial community structure during AD with the addition of NBW, the 
microbial community in the system was analyzed by metagenomic 
sequencing in this study. After quality control, sequence splicing, gene 
prediction and de-redundancy, a total of 2,862,918 valid genes were 
acquired. The results of principal component analysis showed that the 
community distance between NBW treatments and DW was greater on 
day 28 than on day 14 (Fig. S2B), suggesting that the addition of NBW 
consistently drove changes in the composition of the microbial com­
munity and enriched specific microbial taxa.
At the domain level, the bacteria (94.0–98.4%) and archaea 
(1.4–5.7%) were the main dominant domains in all groups on day 28 of 
AD (Fig. S2A), and the proportion of archaea in the NBW treatments 
were 2.3 (Air-NBW), 2.1 (O2-NBW), and 4.1 (O3-NBW) times that in DW, 
respectively, showing that methanogens might be enriched. At the 
phylum level, Euryarchaeota is the dominant group, which is consistent 
with the findings of Fan et al. (2021a). Euryarchaeota is recognized as the 
major methanogenic phylum (Zhang et al., 2020), showed a clear trend 
of increasing relative abundance in all treatment groups. Whether 
incubated for 14 d or 28 d, their relative abundance showed a pattern of

and Fig. 3A). Furthermore, the relative abundance of Euryarchaeota in 
O3-NBW was significantly higher than that in O2-NBW and Air-NBW (P 
< 0.05). This suggests that the addition of O3 NBs may have created a 
more suitable anaerobic environment, providing stable conditions for 
the proliferation of methanogenic archaea (Wang et al., 2017). At the 
same time, O3 NBs may also oxidize complex organic compounds into 
compounds with lower molecular weights and higher bioavailability, 
thereby increasing the substrate available to methanogens, which in 
turn promotes the enrichment of Euryarchaeota. At the genus level, the 
dominant archaeal genus in all samples was Methanothrix, with relative 
abundance ranging from 41.8% to 76.1%, followed by unclassi­
fied_p_Euryarchaeota, Methanobacterium and Methanosarcina, with rela­
tive abundance ranging from 5.3% to 13.9%, 0.5% to 17.7% and 1.1% to 
23.7%, respectively (Fig. 3B). Consistent with findings from previous 
studies, Methanobacterium was also identified as a major genus in the 
present study (Fan et al., 2024). As a hydrogenotrophic methanogen, 
Methanobacterium primarily utilizes CO2 and H2 as energy sources. 
Overall, the combined relative abundance of these four dominant 
methanogenic genera on day 28 increased in the order DW < O2-NBW <
Air-NBW <
O3-NBW, which was consistent with the observed 
enhancement in cumulative methane yield.
At the phylum level, the bacterial communities of all treatment 
groups were dominated by Proteobacteria (25.0–57.8%), Bacteroidetes 
(8.8–20.6%), Chloroflexi (5.6–31.2%), Firmicutes (3.1–14.1%), and 
Actinobacteria (2.2–8.0%) (Fig. 3A). This is consistent with the results of 
previous studies on microorganisms (Zhou et al., 2024). On day 28, the 
relative abundances of Chloroflexi, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Plancto­
mycetes, and Candidatus_Hydrogenedentes in all NBW treatments were 
markedly higher than those observed in DW. Among these taxa, Chlor­
oflexi, which are characterized as filamentous multicellular microor­
ganisms, are known to facilitate carbohydrate hydrolysi (X. Wang et al., 
2020b). Firmicutes can participate in the AD process by secreting 
extracellular enzymes involved in substrate degradation and VFA pro­
duction, which in turn provide suitable precursors for the methanogenic 
process. In addition, Actinobacteria and Candidatus_Hydrogenedentes have 
been shown to have the ability to degrade organic matter, including 
proteins, lipids and polysaccharides (Xiao et al., 2020). Overall, these 
microorganisms are primarily responsible for driving the hydrolysis and 
acidification stages of AD. It is worth noting that their abundance was 
higher in the NBW treatment, suggesting that the introduction of NBs 
may have created a more favorable microenvironment for the hydrolytic 
microbial community, thereby accelerating the breakdown of complex 
organic matter. Furthermore, Planctomycetes, which are commonly 
associated with denitrification processes, showed increased abundance 
under NBW addition. This enrichment may be related to the elevated 
availability of nitrogen released from substrate degradation in the 
presence of NBW, a trend that aligns with the observed variation in TAN 
concentrations (Fig. S1A) (Liang et al., 2021). Consistent patterns were 
also observed at the genus level, where NBW addition resulted in pro­
nounced shifts in bacterial community structure during AD (Fig. S3), in 
agreement with previous studies (Wang et al., 2020a). Compared with 
the control, unclassified_d_Bacteroidales, unclassified_c_Anaerolineae, Len­
timicrobium, and unclassified_c_Deltaproteobacteria were notably enriched 
in the NBW treatments on both day 14 and day 28. Bacteroidales is 
closely related to the process of glucose hydrolysis, and can produce 
acetic acid and propionic acid through the fermentation of saccharides, 
and the two are the main metabolic end-products (Qin et al., 2020). 
Anaerolineae is capable of degrading recalcitrant organic compounds (Li 
et al., 2019). Lentimicrobium is a genus of strictly fermentative bacteria 
capable of converting complex organic matter into VFAs, ethanol and 
H2/CO2 (Zhang et al., 2021a).
3.5. Metagenomic analysis of methane metabolism
To further elucidate how NBW addition reshapes microbial function 
to enhance methanogenesis, we analyzed the abundance of genes 
encoding key enzymes in the three major methanogenic pathways: 
acetoclastic (M00357), hydrogenotrophic (M00567), and methylo­

modules using TPM normalization. The TPM values of genes associated

treatments than in the DW (P < 0.001), indicating a systemic 
enhancement of the microbial methanogenic potential by NBW (Fig. S4).

4. Discussion
4.1. Enhanced methane production and substrate degradation under 
nanobubble treatments
The addition of NBW notably improved the overall efficiency of AD, 
as evidenced by increased methane production and enhanced organic 
matter degradation (Fig. 2). Consistent with previous studies reporting 
that NBs can shorten the start-up phase of AD by accelerating cellulose 
hydrolysis and promoting the formation of VFAs (Fan et al., 2024; Xu 
et al., 2025), our results indicate that NBW treatment offers distinct 
kinetic advantages. Notably, in the O3-NBW, the peak methane yield 
occurred earliest (Fig. 2B), suggesting that NBs effectively alleviated the 
initial lag phase in SW digestion, likely by facilitating a faster transition 
from the hydrolysis stage to the active methane production stage.
The dynamic changes in SCOD and VFAs further reveal this enhanced 
metabolic coupling. In all NBW treatments, the rapid decline in SCOD 
during the first week indicates an accelerated rate of complex organic 
matter degradation (Fig. 2C). Although VFA concentrations rose during 
the initial days (0–7 days), they subsequently dropped sharply (7–14 
days), which coincided with a surge in daily methane production 
(Fig. 2B, 2D). This synchrony suggests that NBW not only increased the 
ultimate methane yield but, more importantly, accelerated the turnover 
of metabolic intermediates. By preventing the excessive accumulation of 
VFA, NBW maintained a more balanced and resilient anaerobic envi­
ronment. By the end, VFA levels were similar across all reactors, sug­
gesting that NBs mainly improved conversion rates of intermediates 
rather than changing the final metabolic endpoints.
A comparative analysis of the treatment of different gases with NBs 
revealed distinct performance strategies. O3-NBW exhibited two distinct

whereas the second peak may be attributed to the subsequent oxidative 
decomposition of refractory organics induced by O3 NBs to be converted 
into substances that can be utilized by microorganisms and metabolized

cumulative methane yield of O3-NBW was approximately 1.52 times 
that of O2-NBW (143.0/94.1). While this ratio coincidentally aligns with 
the stoichiometric ratio of oxygen atoms in O3 versus O2. The distinct 
secondary methane peak, unique to the O3-NBW treatment, indicates 
that the enhanced yield stems from the degradation of a refractory 
organic fraction that O2-NBW was unable to break down. Therefore, we 
attribute the higher methane yield to O3′s superior oxidative capacity 
unlocking an additional carbon source for methanogenesis, not simply a 
direct stoichiometric conversion. This superior performance highlights 
that O3 NBs facilitate the start-up phase in the early stages and appear to 
be more effective than O2 NBs or air NBs in overcoming hydrolysis 
limitations. Interestingly, O2-NBW produced less methane than Air-NBW 
(Fig. 2A), which may be because moderate microaeration stimulates 
facultative microorganisms, but higher dissolved oxygen may shift 
facultative microbes toward aerobic respiration (Costa et al., 2025), 
mineralizing organics to CO2 instead of routing carbon through 
fermentation and methanogenesis (Fu et al., 2023). At the same time, 
methanogens are oxygen-sensitive, so sustained O2 can directly suppress 
their activity (Appels et al., 2008).
In summary, these macroscopic performance results confirm that 
NBW, particularly O3-NBW, act as potent catalysts for AD by acceler­
ating the substrate flux from hydrolysis to methanogenesis. These 
findings provide a performance-based rationale for further investigation 
of the effects of chemical pretreatment (Section 4.2) and the changes in 
microbial communities driven by these unique NBW treatments (Section 
4.3).
4.2. Mechanism of enhanced hydrolysis and acidification by nanobubble 
water
The significant increase in methane yield and COD removal rate in­
dicates that NBs promote the AD process, particularly by enhancing 
hydrolysis and acidification, which are typically considered rate- 
limiting steps. Under various treatment conditions, O3-NBW demon­
strated a more pronounced promotional effect. This is likely due pri­
marily to the strong oxidizing capacity of ozone and the reactive oxygen 
species potentially generated during the collapse of NBs. The high redox 
potential of ozone, along with the hydroxyl radicals (⋅OH) released 
during NB collapse (Varoutoglou et al., 2025), aids in breaking down 
refractory chemical bonds in complex organic compounds that remain 
stable under conventional anaerobic conditions or when exposed to 
oxygen (Koundle et al., 2025). This in-situ chemical pretreatment 
effectively converts non-degradable components into easily oxidizable

unique secondary methane peak observed in the O3-NBW reactor.
In addition to chemical oxidation, the physical properties of NBs may 
also contribute to the sustained transformation of the substrate. Previous 
studies have shown that NBs can remain stable in water for extended 
periods under certain conditions (Ji et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2016), 
although the mechanisms underlying this stability are still under 
investigation. It is generally believed that the stability of NBs is closely 
related to their surface charge, interfacial adsorption layers, and the 
composition of ions and organic matter in the solution. Therefore, in 
complex aqueous systems such as wastewater, the stability of NBs is 
typically influenced by ionic strength, and dissolved organic matter. 
Although we attempted to monitor NB characteristics during AD, the 
high turbidity and complex particulate/biological background of the 
reactor matrix caused severe analytical interference, preventing reliable 
real-time determination of NB size and concentration. In this study, 
methane production and substrate degradation showed an upward trend 
(as shown in Section 4.1), while the microbial community structure also 
exhibited certain functional adaptations (as described in Section 4.3). 
These phenomena suggest, to some extent, that the introduction of NBs 
produces sustained functional effects in the AD system. Their nanoscale 
size results in extremely low buoyancy, significantly prolonging their 
residence time within the reactor (Favvas et al., 2021). Additionally, the 
typically negative charge on the surface of NBs (high zeta potential) 
effectively inhibits coalescence and premature dissolution through 
electrostatic repulsion (Wang and Lu, 2025). These physicochemical 
characteristics may contribute to the persistence of NBs after introduc­
tion into complex systems However, the in situ direct monitoring of NB 
size and concentration in AD under conditions of high suspended solids 
concentration remains a significant technical challenge in this field 
(Chuenchart et al., 2021; Fan et al., 2021b; Jia et al., 2023; Wang et al., 
2023). Therefore, the size evolution and concentration changes of NBs 
throughout the entire AD process, as well as their relationship with 
enhanced treatment effects, require further investigation.
Unlike macro-bubbles, NBs possess an extremely high specific sur­
face area and mass transfer efficiency, which significantly increases the 
frequency of contact between enzymes and substrates (Wang et al., 
2026). O3 NBs also tend to carry a strongly negative zeta potential, so 
electrostatic repulsion limits coalescence and helps them remain stable 
(Singh et al., 2024). According to the literature, thanks to this stability, 
O3 NBs in such systems may have contributed to maintain dissolved 
oxygen at a relatively low level of approximately 0.2–1.0 mg/L, thereby 
creating a sustained micro-oxidative environment (Tsai et al., 2025). 
This environment provides optimal conditions for facultative hydrolytic 
bacteria, allowing them to function normally over time without 
adversely affecting strict methanogens.
More fundamentally, the high interfacial free energy of the nega­
tively charged surfaces of NBs reduces the surface tension of the 
wastewater matrix. This physical modification alters the surface prop­
erties of particulate organic matter, making it more susceptible to mi­
crobial attachment (Yasui et al., 2019). By promoting bacterial 
attachment to solid surfaces, NBW facilitates the formation of robust 
biofilms and enhances the spatial proximity between hydrolytic en­
zymes and complex substrates. These combined physical and chemical 
mechanisms collectively accelerate the carbon transfer from particulate 
organic matter to volatile fatty acids, thereby supporting a significant 
improvement in overall digestion performance.
4.3. Impact of nanobubble water on microbial community and 
methanogenic pathways
In addition to improved substrate conversion, NBW treatment was 
accompanied by changes in microbial community structure and 
methanogenesis-related functional genes. These changes showed good 
correlation with increased methane production, suggesting that NBW 
treatment may have further influenced the methane production process 
within the system. However, it should be noted that these biological 
responses more likely reflect adaptive adjustments resulting from 
improved substrate availability and changes in the reaction 
microenvironment.
In this study, we found that the abundance of certain genes associ­
ated with electron transfer-related structures (such as PilA and OmcS) 
decreased in the NBW treatments (Fig. S5), while methane production 
increased simultaneously. This phenomenon suggests that NBW treat­
ment may have altered the electron transport strategy within the system 
and reduced the genetic investment in certain energy-intensive biolog­
ical conductive structures. We speculate that the interfacial electrical 
properties and surface characteristics of NBs may have influenced the 
spatial contact or electron transfer resistance among symbiotic micro­
organisms to some extent, thereby reducing the microbial community’s 
investment in structures such as conductive pili and redirecting more 
metabolic resources toward the methanogenesis process. This phenom­
enon is consistent with observations in systems where inorganic 
conductive materials were added (Worajo et al., 2025).
Changes in the microbial community provide indirect support for the 
above hypothesis. The significant enrichment of Methanothrix during 
NBW treatment suggests that a microbial community structure more 
conducive to efficient methane production may have formed (Fig. 3B). 
Because Methanothrix is a typical methanogenic archaeon, it is able to 
receive electrons directly through DIET and reduce CO2 to methane 
(Zhao et al., 2020). Liu et al. similarly found that NBs promote the 
enrichment of Syntrophomonas, a bacterium which, like Methanothrix, is 
a typical DIET-functioning microorganism (Liu et al., 2024). These 
community changes suggest that NBW treatment is associated with 
community restructuring related to electron transfer.
NBW treatment was also accompanied by an enhancement of mul­
tiple methane-producing pathways, shifting from the predominant 
acetoclastic methanogenic pathway to a synergistic, multi-pathway 
metabolic network. Although acetoclastic methanogenic pathway re­
mains the primary pathway for methane production, the gene abun­
dance of key enzymes in the hydrogenotrophic and methylotrophic 
pathways increased significantly following NBW treatment. This shift in 
metabolic pattern may be related to enhanced substrate availability and 
improved mass transfer efficiency.
Particularly under O3-NBW, stronger oxidative effects may promote 
the conversion of some recalcitrant organic compounds into small- 
molecule organic acids, fermentable sugars, and other intermediate 
metabolites, thereby providing a richer substrate source for various 
methanogenic pathways (Auma Omondi and Aluda Kegode, 2023; Fan 
et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2021) At the same time, NBs may further 
enhance the synergy among multiple methane-producing pathways by 
improving gas–liquid mass transfer and the local hydrogen transfer 
environment (Chuenchart et al., 2021). This metabolic flexibility is re­
flected to some extent in the microbial community structure. The 
abundance of the Methanosarcina serves as an example; its ability to 
utilize acetate, hydrogen/carbon dioxide, and methyl compounds 
demonstrates the community’s adaptability to multi-pathway strategies.
It is worth noting that, although these results support an association 
between NBW treatment and the restructuring of the methanogenic 
network, this study cannot yet strictly distinguish whether this biolog­
ical response stems from the direct effects of NBs on microorganisms or 
from indirect effects resulting from the physicochemical transformation 
of substrates. Combined with the results in Section 4.2, the current ev­
idence more directly supports the hypothesis that O3-NBW first im­
proves substrate availability by enhancing the transformation of 
complex organic matter, while changes in microbial communities and 
functional genes are more likely to be subsequent responses to these 
substrate and environmental changes. Therefore, whether NBs directly 
stimulate microbial metabolism still requires further verification 
through more discriminatory experimental designs, such as establishing 
gas-specific NBW treatment systems containing only wastewater or only 
inoculated sludge, respectively, to distinguish between substrate effects

4.4. Practical Implications and Future Perspectives
The findings of this study provide key insights into the application of 
NB technology in the sustainable management of SW, demonstrating the 
potential of NBs to transform the conventional AD process into a highly 
efficient resource recovery process. Integrating O3-NBW into AD systems 
offers significant economic and environmental benefits. By promoting 
efficient methanogenesis through enhanced hydrolysis, O3-NBW nearly 
doubles the energy recovered per unit of reactor volume. This 
improvement directly enhances the project’s economic viability by 
increasing biogas revenue and potentially reducing net treatment costs 
through reduced sludge treatment and shorter retention times. These 
findings are highly aligned with global strategic goals for resource re­
covery and carbon neutrality in the agricultural sector.
Beyond organics, swine wastewater often carries residual antibiotics 
and disinfectants that suppress AD microbiology. O3 NBs may also 
reduce this inhibition by oxidizing such biotoxic compounds in situ, 
improving effluent safety, easing the load on downstream processes, and 
lowering ecological risks after discharge. Although O3 NBs technology 
shows good potential for application, its practical engineering applica­
tion still faces many challenges. Future research should focus on 
advancing the scaled-up development of NBs generation systems and 
exploring their long-term operational stability under different climatic 
conditions and feedstock components. In addition, in-depth study of the 
synergistic effect of NBs and other process enhancements, including 
inoculation of functional microbial for biological enhancement, com­
bined with solar thermal technology, can open up a new direction for the 
research and development of intelligent, near-zero emission sewage 
treatment system for livestock and poultry breeding industry.
5. Conclusion
This study shows that adding nanobubble water to anaerobic 
digestion of swine wastewater markedly increases methane recovery, 
with O3-NBW giving the greatest improvement (87.5%). The process 
shifts from purely biological conversion to a synergistic mechanism in 
which nanobubbles enhance hydrolysis and change the electron transfer 
strategy. This is supported by the enrichment of Methanothrix and the 
downregulation of the energy-demanding pilA gene. Because the 
experiment lasted 28 days, longer runs (60–90 days) are required to 
evaluate microbial community stability and confirm whether O3-NBW 
advantages persist.
From an engineering viewpoint, O3-NBW can provide in situ pre­
treatment while stimulating metabolic activity, potentially shortening 
hydraulic retention time, reducing reactor footprint, and improving on- 
farm energy self-sufficiency via higher biogas yields. However, scale-up 
faces challenges. O3 generation is energy-intensive and needs special­
ized equipment, raising capital and operating costs. Nanobubble pro­
duction via high-pressure dissolution requires robust pumps and 
accurate pressure control, adding further energy demand. In addition, 
while ozone can break down complex organics, excessive dosing may 
create oxidative stress and inhibit strict anaerobic methanogens during 
long-term continuous operation.
Future studies should conduct techno-economic analysis and life- 
cycle assessment to determine whether extra methane production off­
sets the energy required for ozone and nanobubble generation. Work is 
also needed to test electron transfer stability in continuous reactors and 
explore synergy between nanobubbles and conductive carbon materials 
(e.g., biochar), thereby further improving efficiency and stability of NB- 
AD systems.
